sections.title: Bank Operating Metrics
sections.subtitle: Cash earnings, efficiency, credit quality and the funding base -- the KPIs a bank is judged on beyond statutory net income

charts.title: Statutory Net Income vs Cash Earnings
Credit Expenses
charts.annotation: Negative values are net impairment releases (write-backs), not charges.

cashEarnings.title: Statutory net income vs cash earnings
cashEarnings.content:
Cash earnings is the bank's own preferred profit measure: statutory net income adjusted for items management judges non-operating (hedge timing, amortisation of intangibles, one-off gains/losses). It is what dividends and guidance are typically framed against.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: FY2025 statutory net income was negative (-$97.1m) while cash earnings was a positive $514.6m -- the gap is one-off items (impairments/write-downs), not a sign the underlying business lost money.

What to watch:

  • A widening, persistent gap between the two lines rather than a single-year one-off
  • Whether cash-earnings addbacks recur every year (then they are not really one-off)

costToIncome.title: Cost-to-income ratio
costToIncome.content:
Cost-to-income is operating expenses divided by operating income -- the standard bank efficiency measure. Lower is better.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the ratio has drifted from the mid-50s (FY2023) to the low 60s (FY2025-26) as margin pressure and technology/compliance spend outpaced income growth -- worse than the major banks' typical low-50s.

What to watch:

  • Direction of travel more than the absolute level -- a bank re-platforming (e.g. cloud migration) should see this fall over time
  • Whether income or cost is driving a change in the ratio

roe.title: Return on equity
roe.content:
ROE is statutory net income divided by average shareholders' equity -- the return generated on shareholders' capital.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: ROE has run roughly 7.3%-8.6% across FY2021-26, below its cost of equity and well under the major banks' low-double-digit ROE -- the central reason the stock trades near or below book value.

What to watch:

  • Whether ROE closes the gap to cost of equity over the forecast period
  • NIM and cost-to-income are the two biggest levers on this number

loansDeposits.title: Net loans vs deposits
loansDeposits.content:
Net loans is the bank's lending book after provisions; deposits is customer deposit funding. Deposits above loans means the bank is funded primarily by customers rather than wholesale markets.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: deposits have tracked slightly above net loans through FY2023-26 (both growing ~3-4% p.a.), a conservative, low wholesale-funding-reliance profile typical of a regional bank.

What to watch:

  • Loan growth materially outpacing deposit growth (rising wholesale funding reliance)
  • The loan-to-deposit ratio trend, not just the absolute levels

creditExpenses.title: Credit expenses
creditExpenses.content:
Credit expenses is the net impairment charge (or release) on the loan book for the period -- the cost of credit quality deteriorating, or a write-back when it improves.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the line has swung from a $33.6m charge (FY2023) to a $14.7m net release (FY2025), reflecting a benign credit cycle rather than a structural improvement in the book.

What to watch:

  • A shift from releases back to charges as the credit cycle turns
  • Credit expenses as a share of the loan book (basis points), not just the dollar figure

capitalLiquidity.title: Regulatory capital and liquidity
capitalLiquidity.content:
CET1 ratio is core equity capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets -- the primary APRA solvency measure. LCR and NSFR are short- and long-term liquidity coverage ratios; both must stay at or above 100% under APRA rules.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: CET1 has held around 11.0-11.4%, comfortably above APRA's ~10.25% "unquestionably strong" benchmark, with LCR (132-140%) and NSFR (~115%) well clear of their 100% floors -- capital is not a constraint on the dividend or buyback capacity here.

What to watch:

  • CET1 trending toward the regulatory minimum rather than away from it
  • A capital raise or dividend cut signalled if any ratio compresses sharply

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
NIM is net interest income as a percentage of interest-earning assets.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the core profitability metric of a lender; a few basis points move earnings materially.

What to watch:

  • NIM trend with the rate cycle
  • Funding cost versus lending yield

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Bendigo and Adelaide Bank Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
